The pattern is a hash map from each id to the last index where it appeared: for each element, ask a question about the elements before it, then record the element. The words that point to it are "already appeared", a question about earlier elements that a nested loop would answer in O(n·k).

A sliding window works too, and is a fair answer: keep the ids of the last k positions in a

The pattern is a fixed-size sliding window with a table of counts. The words that point to it are "substring", which means contiguous, and a length fixed by
. Two substrings are anagrams exactly when their byte counts are equal, so the window keeps the counts of its bytes and compares them with the pattern's:

Comparing two tables of 256 counts costs 256 steps, so the whole run is 256·n steps, which is O(n) for a fixed alphabet, and the space is O(1) besides the output. To make each step O(1), keep a count of the byte values whose counts differ between
, and update it only for the byte that enters and the byte that leaves. The edge cases are a pattern longer than the text, overlapping matches as in
, and a match that ends on the last byte of the text.
Sorting every substring and comparing it with the sorted pattern is correct and costs O(n·m log m). It earns the second point only if you named that cost before coding.

Write down, for each problem, the pattern you named before coding, whether it worked, the words in the statement that should have told you, your time, and your score out of 3. Add one line on the mistake you most want not to repeat. You pass this set when you earned the first two points on all three problems. A problem where you named the wrong pattern goes back on your list: re-solve it closed book in a week.
